content: Allopurinol is a medication prescribed to treat gout, elevated uric acid levels caused by certain cancer treatments, and kidney stones. It belongs to a class of drugs known as xanthine oxidase inhibitors. This medication works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body, as high levels of uric acid can lead to gout attacks or kidney stones. It is important to note that allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks and is not effective for treating an acute gout attack once it has started. Allopurinol is available in tablet form and is taken orally, typically once or twice daily, preferably after meals. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed, without altering the dose or frequency. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it, usually no more than once per week. It may take several months or longer to experience the full benefits of allopurinol. During the initial months of treatment, you may experience an increase in gout attacks, but this will subside over time as the medication prevents future attacks. Your doctor may prescribe an additional medication, such as colchicine, to help prevent gout attacks during the first few months of allopurinol therapy. Continue taking allopurinol even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. In addition to its primary uses, allopurinol is sometimes prescribed for other conditions, such as seizures, pain associated with pancreatic disease, and certain infections. It may also be used to improve survival after bypass surgery, reduce the recurrence of ulcers, and prevent kidney transplant rejection. If your doctor prescribes allopurinol for an off-label use, discuss the potential risks and benefits with them. Before starting allopurinol, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to allopurinol or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as certain medications may interact with allopurinol. Examples include amoxicillin, ampicillin, anticoagulants like warfarin, chemotherapy drugs such as cyclophosphamide and mercaptopurine, chlorpropamide, diuretics, immunosuppressants like azathioprine and cyclosporine, other gout medications like probenecid and sulfinpyrazone, and tolbutamide. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, heart failure, or if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking allopurinol, notify your doctor immediately. Be aware that allopurinol may cause drowsiness, so avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how the medication affects you. Ask your doctor about the safe consumption of alcohol while on allopurinol, as alcohol may reduce the medication's effectiveness. While taking allopurinol, it is important to stay hydrated by drinking at least eight glasses of water or other fluids daily, unless otherwise directed by your doctor. If you miss a dose of allopurinol, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Allopurinol may cause side effects. Common, less severe side effects include upset stomach, diarrhea, and drowsiness. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Rare but serious side effects include skin rash, painful urination, blood in the urine, eye irritation, swelling of the lips or mouth, fever, sore throat, chills, signs of infection, loss of appetite, unexpected weight loss, and itching. If you experience any of these severe symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. Report any unusual problems or serious side effects to your doctor or the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store allopurinol in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture, and do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. Keep all medical and laboratory appointments while taking allopurinol, as your doctor will need to monitor your response to the medication through regular tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription. Allopurinol is sold under the brand names Aloprim® and Zyloprim®.
